node-1.label: Patient presented with stridor, increased work of breathing, and supplemental oxygen requirement

node-2.label: Patient was transferred from an outside hospital to the ED after falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth several hours earlier; he did not remember the exact cause of the fall and believed he may have lost consciousness.

node-3.label: Physical examination in the ED showed diffuse supraglottic edema most severe in the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, which obstructed the view of the true vocal cords.

why.why: Radiologist analysis confirms CT shows glottic and supraglottic swelling without fractures and direct laryngoscopy shows diffuse edema with mucosal sloughing, directly verifying supraglottic obstruction. Combined with the initial physical examination and endoscopic findings, these data remain strongly consistent with supraglottic edema as the final common pathway for stridor and increased work of breathing. Confidence remains very high, adjusted slightly to 0.96.

Radiologist analysis reinforces trauma/burn from e-cigarette: CT shows no fractures and direct laryngoscopy shows mucosal sloughing, while esophageal scar and antral ulceration support a caustic/thermal injury mechanism rather than infection. The fall with an e-cigarette in the mouth provides the exposure history. These findings increase confidence from 0.85 to 0.9.

Radiologist analysis notes that inflammatory markers and culture results are unavailable, so infectious supraglottitis cannot be fully excluded. This new evidence modestly increases the likelihood from 0.05 to 0.1. However, the traumatic e-cigarette exposure, CT/laryngoscopy findings, and esophageal scar/antral ulceration still argue strongly against infection, so confidence remains low.
